question: In France, the prison occupancy rate stood at an average of 140 % as at 1 July, rising to as high as 170 % in remand centres. Conditions being such, prisoners are forced to share cells measuring around ten square metres with three or even four other inmates. During the heatwave, temperatures in some of these cells rose to nearly 57 °C, as was notably the case in Nimes.

Whilst prisoners are forced by law to serve a prison sentence, the appalling conditions in which they are being held are not part of that sentence. The European Convention on Human Rights prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment and sets out minimum standards of detention. However, nothing is being done at European level to ensure these minimum standards of detention are being met. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission intend to take the necessary measures to ensure respect for human rights in European prisons through the establishment of a framework setting out minimum conditions for detention?
Does it intend to put in place the necessary measures to monitor whether human rights in European prisons are being respected?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.9.2026) Detention issues fall primarily within the responsibility of the Member States. To complement and support Member States’ policies, on 8 December 2022, the Commission adopted the Recommendation on the procedural rights of suspects and accused in pre-trial detention and on material detention conditions1.

On the basis of the Recommendation, Member States should ensure that detainees are treated with respect and dignity and in line with human rights obligations, including the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment as laid down in Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 4 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.

Moreover, the Recommendation provides specific guidance on the minimum standards to be followed by Member States for material detention conditions, including in relation to accommodation, healthcare, nutrition and time spent outside the cell and outdoors.

By the end of 2026, the Commission will publish a comprehensive report assessing the national measures taken by the Member States to follow-up to the Recommendation. The Commission will then be able to evaluate how each Member State is performing and, where implementation falls short, will be better placed to consider how to address any remaining issues.
1 Commission Recommendation (EU) 2023/681 of 8 December 2022 on procedural rights of suspects and
accused persons subject to pre-trial detention and on material detention conditions, OJ L 86, 24.3.2023, pp. 44– 57.
